title: Project Overview
description: Start with README.md to understand the project's purpose: a synthetic research panel where five opinionated AI personas debate and score any idea in real time. This document outlines the multi-stage workflow — Moderator Intro, Independent Responses, Follow-up, Discussion, Voting, and Synthesis — and maps the technology stack (FastAPI + Google ADK on the backend, Next.js 16 + React 19 on the frontend, SSE for real-time streaming). Reading it first gives you the mental model that makes every subsequent file meaningful. AGENTS.md supplements this with agent-specific conventions for the Google ADK integration.

title: Data Models and Schemas
description: The data layer defines the shared vocabulary for the entire system. state.py holds the TypedDict that flows through the ADK workflow graph — every agent node reads from and writes to this shared state object. schemas.py defines the Pydantic models used for API request/response validation, establishing the contract between the FastAPI layer and external callers. Understanding these two files first prevents confusion when reading how agents and API routes interact with the same data structures.
languageLesson: Python TypedDict (from the `typing` module) provides static type hints for dictionary-shaped data without runtime overhead, while Pydantic models add runtime validation and serialization. The two are complementary: TypedDict for internal workflow state, Pydantic for external API boundaries.

title: AI Persona Definitions
description: personas.py is where the five AI identities live: the Skeptical Investor, Early Adopter, Enterprise CTO, UX Researcher, and Growth Marketer. Each persona is defined with a distinct system prompt, scoring rubric, and personality archetype that shapes how its underlying Gemini model responds. This file is the creative and behavioral heart of the project — the personas here are what make the debate feel like a real focus group rather than a generic chatbot response.

title: ADK Workflow Graph
description: graph.py wires the workflow together using the Google ADK's graph primitives. It declares the sequence of nodes — moderator intro, parallel participant responses, moderator follow-up, parallel discussion, voting, and synthesis — and connects them with conditional and sequential edges. This file is the architectural blueprint of the focus group session: it determines what runs, in what order, and which steps run in parallel. Reading it alongside the persona definitions from Step 3 reveals how the ADK dispatches work to each agent.
languageLesson: Google ADK workflow graphs use a declarative node-and-edge model similar to a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Parallel fan-out steps allow multiple agent nodes to execute concurrently, which is how all five personas respond simultaneously in the Independent Responses phase.

title: Agent Nodes
description: The three node files implement the actual agent logic invoked by the graph. moderator.py manages the focus group — it writes the opening prompt and the follow-up probes that steer the discussion. participant.py is the generic node that each of the five personas runs through: it receives the shared state, appends its persona's voice, and emits a score. synthesizer.py runs last, aggregating all participant outputs into a coherent final report. Together, these three files translate the abstract graph topology from Step 4 into concrete LLM calls.

title: Backend API Layer
description: main.py is the FastAPI entry point: it mounts the routers, configures CORS, and starts the application. sessions.py handles the session lifecycle — creating a new focus group run, storing session state, and cleaning up after completion. Together they form the HTTP layer that the frontend talks to, translating REST calls into ADK workflow invocations and making the state defined in Step 2 available across requests.

title: SSE Streaming
description: stream.py implements the Server-Sent Events endpoint that pushes real-time agent output to the browser as it is generated. Instead of waiting for all five agents to finish, the client receives events incrementally — each persona's message, score, and status update arrives as it happens. This file is the bridge between the async ADK workflow (Step 4) and the live frontend experience. It converts internal state mutations into a stream of JSON events the React hook (Step 9) consumes.
languageLesson: Server-Sent Events (SSE) use a persistent HTTP connection where the server pushes `data: <json>\n\n` lines to the client. Unlike WebSockets, SSE is unidirectional and works over standard HTTP/2, making it ideal for streaming LLM output without the complexity of a full duplex channel.

title: Security Plugins
description: The plugins layer adds trust monitoring and enforcement on top of the agent workflow. blue_team_plugin.py observes agent outputs and computes trust scores based on consistency, tone, and adherence to persona constraints. green_team_plugin.py acts on those scores: when an agent's trust score drops below a threshold it quarantines that agent, preventing its output from influencing the final synthesis. This stateful guardrail system ensures the focus group remains methodologically sound even if a model produces anomalous responses.
languageLesson: Plugin architectures in ADK allow cross-cutting concerns (logging, safety, monitoring) to be injected into the workflow without modifying individual node logic. Blue Team (observe/score) and Green Team (enforce/quarantine) is a pattern borrowed from security red-team/blue-team exercises applied here to AI reliability.

title: Frontend Types and State Hook
description: frontend/app/types/index.ts defines the TypeScript interfaces that mirror the backend Pydantic schemas from Step 2 — AgentMessage, SessionState, Score, and FinalReport — giving the frontend full type safety over SSE payloads. useFocusGroup.ts is the central React hook that manages all client-side session state: it opens the SSE connection to stream.py, parses incoming events, and exposes typed state plus action dispatchers to every UI component. All React components receive their data from this single hook, making it the frontend equivalent of the ADK workflow graph.
languageLesson: Centralizing SSE consumption in a single custom hook (`useFocusGroup`) is the React equivalent of a state machine. It prevents multiple components from independently opening SSE connections and ensures that all derived state updates are co-located, making the data flow easy to trace.

title: UI Components and Entry Page
description: The UI layer assembles the experience. layout.tsx wraps the app with global fonts and metadata. page.tsx is the Next.js root page that composes all components and calls useFocusGroup. TopicInput.tsx captures the user's idea and submits it to start a session. DiscussionThread.tsx and AgentBubble.tsx render the live debate as messages stream in. ScorePanel.tsx displays each persona's running score, and FinalReport.tsx renders the synthesized conclusion with export buttons powered by exportReport.ts, which generates PDF and Word documents entirely client-side using jsPDF and the docx library.
languageLesson: Client-side document generation (jsPDF, docx) runs entirely in the browser without a server round-trip, which keeps the backend stateless and avoids storing user report data on the server. This pattern trades server resource usage for client CPU — acceptable here because reports are generated once per session.
